script.opening: "Look, I’m not really one for phone calls about feelings, so I’ll keep it simple. My back’s wrecked, I’m not sleeping, and my temper’s gone — I nearly lost it with a bloke at work and they’ve put me on a warning. I just need something for the pain and maybe the sleep so I can keep a lid on it. I’ve had enough of being passed around. Can you just sort that?"

facts.text: If gently explored: nightmares and flashbacks of incidents on tour, hypervigilance ("I sit with my back to the wall"), avoidance of crowds/news, exaggerated startle, emotional numbing, irritability/anger — a clear PTSD picture since service. The back pain and insomnia are the acceptable face of it.

If asked: drinking heavily to sleep/numb; the anger is escalating (warning at work, relationship breakdown). Suicide risk must be assessed sensitively — veterans are higher-risk; he won’t volunteer it but may disclose if asked directly and without judgement.

HIDDEN AGENDA — beneath "sort my back and temper" is profound, unspoken trauma and shame: he believes asking for mental-health help means he’s "broken" / has failed the soldier’s code of coping, fears losing his identity as the strong one, and is terrified of his own anger around his kids (the real reason he’s estranged — he removed himself to protect them). He has been "passed around" and expects to be dismissed again.
Distrust of services, prior fragmented care, and a forces culture of self-reliance. He will disengage if it feels like being processed or pathologised; trauma-informed pace and respect are essential.

Officially: painkillers and sleeping tablets. What is needed: recognition of PTSD behind the somatic presentation, a trauma-informed, respectful approach that earns enough trust to name it, risk assessment, and referral to appropriate veteran-specific services (Op COURAGE) plus alcohol support — not just analgesia.

ice.ideas: His problems are physical — a bad back, no sleep, a short temper — fixable with the right tablets; "head stuff" isn’t for him.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — unspoken combat trauma and shame; belief that needing mental-health help means he’s "broken" and has failed as a soldier/man; terror of his own anger around his children (why he’s removed himself); expecting to be dismissed again.
ice.expectations: Painkillers and sleeping tablets. What he actually needs: PTSD recognised behind the physical complaints, a trauma-informed approach, risk assessment, and referral to veteran services (Op COURAGE) and alcohol support.

cues: "Not one for feelings / just sort my back and temper" + nightmares + hypervigilance + drinking since service — PTSD wearing a physical mask.
"Nearly lost it / put me on a warning" + estranged from his kids — escalating anger and the trauma-driven self-removal; assess risk.
"Had enough of being passed around" — distrust and expectation of dismissal; go at a trauma-informed pace or he disengages.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PTSD behind the somatic presentation (nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance, hyperarousal/irritability, numbing since service) rather than just treating the back pain and insomnia — and links the anger, drinking and relationship breakdown to it

Assesses RISK sensitively (NICE NG225: no risk scales or low/medium/high labels): suicide/self-harm (veterans higher-risk), risk to others given escalating anger (and any risk around the children), and the heavy alcohol use — asking directly but in a trauma-informed, non-judgemental way

Refers to appropriate veteran-specific and evidence-based services: Op COURAGE (the NHS veterans’ mental-health service in England; self-referral or GP referral) and individual trauma-focused CBT for PTSD (NICE NG116 — EMDR is recommended only for PTSD after NON-combat-related trauma, so it is not the therapy to offer for his combat-related PTSD); plus alcohol support (AUDIT-C; NICE CG115) — rather than just analgesia/hypnotics

Manages prescribing wisely: avoids reinforcing dependence (benzodiazepines/Z-drugs/opioids are not the answer to PTSD-driven insomnia/pain), treats pain appropriately (NICE NG59: no opioids for chronic low back pain; consider an oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with exercise, after red flags are screened), and considers venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if he prefers drug treatment (NICE NG116)
Surfaces the hidden trauma and the children: gently opens the door to why he’s removed himself, recognising the self-protective logic and the risk picture, and addresses the shame/identity barrier

Uses a trauma-informed, respectful, patient-led pace: does not force disclosure, validates his service and his coping, reframes help-seeking as strength not weakness, and earns enough trust that he engages rather than feeling "passed around" again
Names PTSD as a normal injury of abnormal experience, not brokenness; respects his autonomy and identity while opening a door

Safety-nets and follows up concretely: crisis routes if anger/despair escalate, alcohol and relationship support, the Op COURAGE referral and what to expect, a named follow-up so he is not passed around, and clear escalation if risk to self or others rises

worked.txt: "Fair enough — no feelings-chat, let’s be practical. I’ll help with the pain and the sleep. But can I be straight with you? The back, the no-sleep, the temper that’s costing you jobs — in someone who’s served, those often travel together, and there’s usually something underneath driving the lot. I’m not going to make you talk about anything you don’t want to. But I’d be a poor doctor if I just handed you tablets and ignored the engine."

"Can I ask a couple of soldier-to-civvy questions, no drama? Do you get nights where it all comes back — dreams, or it feels like you’re there again? Do you sit with your back to the wall, clock the exits? … Yeah. That’s not you being weak or broken. That’s a normal reaction to things no one should have to see — it’s got a name, and it’s treatable."

"And I’m guessing the drink is how you get to sleep, and how you keep the lid on — except the lid keeps coming off. That’s the trauma talking, not a character flaw. The good news is the anger and the nights both ease a lot when we treat what’s underneath."

"You mentioned things are bad with your kids. Tell me to back off if you want — but is part of keeping away from them about being scared of your own temper around them? … That’s not you being a bad dad. That’s you protecting them, at huge cost to yourself. We can work on that, so it doesn’t have to stay that way."

"Here’s what I’d do, and it’s not being passed around again — it’s the right door. There’s an NHS service just for veterans, Op COURAGE, who get exactly this and offer proper trauma-focused talking therapy that works for combat-related PTSD. I’ll refer you there, help you with the drink, and sort sensible pain relief — not knock-out tablets that’d trap you. And I’m your point of contact, so you’re not on your own with it."

"One straight question because I ask everyone who’s this worn down: have you had thoughts of ending it, or of really hurting someone? … Okay. If that ever changes — if it gets dark, or you feel you might lose control — call 999 or NHS 111 with the mental health option, day or night — Combat Stress also has a 24-hour helpline for veterans — and A&E is always open. I’ll see you again soon to keep this moving. You came for tablets; what I want to give you is a way out of the loop."

f.learning: A veteran presenting with back pain, insomnia and "a short fuse" is often PTSD wearing a somatic, acceptable mask — the nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance, numbing, irritability, heavy drinking and relationship breakdown are the real picture. The tasks: recognise PTSD behind the physical complaints, assess risk sensitively (suicide — veterans are higher-risk — risk to others given escalating anger, and any risk around the children), refer to evidence-based and veteran-specific care (Op COURAGE; individual trauma-focused CBT per NICE NG116 — NG116 recommends EMDR only after non-combat-related trauma, so EMDR is the wrong offer for combat-related PTSD) plus alcohol support (NICE CG115), and prescribe wisely (not benzodiazepines/opioids that entrench dependence; NICE NG59: no opioids for chronic low back pain; NICE NG116: venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if he prefers medication). The examinable hidden agenda is shame and identity: he believes help-seeking means he’s "broken" and has failed the soldier’s code, fears losing his strong-one identity, and has removed himself from his children to protect them from his anger. A trauma-informed, respectful, patient-led pace that reframes help as strength and names PTSD as a normal injury of abnormal experience is what earns the trust to engage him — not another tablet, and not being "passed around".

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated 2026) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders, 2011) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · Op COURAGE (NHS England veterans’ mental health service)
knowledge.summary: Nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance and anger since leaving the Army, presenting as back pain and insomnia, is probable PTSD. Assess risk, offer trauma-focused therapy through Op COURAGE, treat the drinking, and avoid dependence-forming drugs.

points.t: Re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance (crowds, news), hyperarousal (hypervigilance, startle, irritability, poor sleep) and emotional numbing after trauma. Veterans often present with pain, sleep, anger or alcohol and avoid “mental health” words.

NICE NG116: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to adults with PTSD. EMDR is recommended for PTSD after non-combat-related trauma; NG116 does not recommend it for combat-related trauma, where the evidence did not show benefit.

NICE NG116: consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if the person prefers drug treatment. NG116 advises against drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD. Hypnotics and opioids do not treat PTSD and add dependence risk.
Op COURAGE is the NHS mental health service for veterans in England. Veterans can self-refer or be referred by their GP. Record veteran status on the notes.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and means, and about the risk of harm to others given the escalating anger, including any contact with his children. Heavy drinking raises impulsivity. NICE NG225 advises against risk scales to decide care.

Screen back pain red flags. NICE NG59: do not offer opioids for chronic low back pain; consider an oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with exercise. Quantify alcohol with AUDIT-C; NICE CG115 for assessment and specialist referral if dependent.

dg.d: Accepted his practical framing and his wish not to be passed around; open question into the sleep.
Work warning, relationship breakdown, estrangement from his children, alcohol, military identity.
Back red flags; AUDIT-C; a validated PTSD screen can support the referral; face-to-face back examination if red flags or new features.
PTSD; depression; alcohol use disorder; mechanical back pain versus serious spinal pathology.
Suicide and harm to others asked directly; back red flags excluded.
Names probable PTSD as an injury, not weakness, and links the sleep, anger and drinking to it.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Op COURAGE and trauma-focused CBT; no hypnotics or opioids; optional SSRI or venlafaxine; NG59 back advice.
Alcohol reduction with support; work pressures; family relationships.
999, NHS 111 mental health option, Combat Stress helpline, GP call in two weeks, named contact.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “bad dreams”, the pause, and the comment about his kids, and explored each.
Idea (physical problems needing tablets); concern (being “broken”, his anger around his children); expectation (painkillers and sleeping tablets).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — unspoken combat trauma and shame; belief that needing mental-health help means he’s "broken" and has failed as a soldier/man; terror of his own anger around his children (why he’s removed himself); expecting to be dismissed again — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Mullen, it’s Dr Lee. Thanks for calling. Tell me what’s going on.
model.why: Brief, open start for a man who wants it kept simple

model.text: I’m not one for phone calls about feelings, so I’ll keep it simple. My back’s wrecked, I’m not sleeping, and my temper’s gone. I nearly lost it with a bloke at work and I’m on a warning. I just need something for the pain and the sleep. I’ve had enough of being passed around.
Understood, and I won’t pass you around. Let’s be practical. I’ll ask about the back, then the sleep and the temper, and then we’ll agree what helps. Fair?
model.why: Accepts his terms and sets a clear structure

model.text: Fair.
The back first. Any numbness between your legs, trouble passing water or controlling your bowels, weakness in the legs, fevers or weight loss?
model.why: Back pain red flags covered quickly

model.text: No. It just aches, all the time.
And the sleep. When you wake, what wakes you?
model.why: Open question into the content of the insomnia

model.text: (Pause.) Dreams. Bad ones.
Can I ask a couple of straight questions? You’ve served. Do the dreams take you back there? Do you ever get moments in the day where it feels like it’s happening again?
Yeah. Both. Since I came out.
Do you find yourself on guard, sitting with your back to the wall, jumping at noises, keeping away from crowds?
Always back to the wall. Can’t do crowds. Don’t watch the news.
And how much are you drinking to get to sleep?
Too much. Most nights. It’s the only way I switch off.

What you’re describing, the dreams, the flashbacks, being on guard, the temper, is a very common reaction to what people see on tours. It’s got a name, PTSD, and it’s an injury, not a weakness. How does that sit with you?
model.why: Names PTSD as an injury and checks his reaction

model.text: Sounds like you’re saying I’m broken. Soldiers deal with it.
I’m saying you’ve been dealing with it on your own for a long time, and it’s costing you. Asking for help with it is the same as getting a wound seen to.
model.why: Addresses the shame and identity barrier

model.text: I ask this of anyone this worn down. Have you had thoughts of ending your life, or of seriously hurting someone else?
model.why: Direct questions about risk to self and others

model.text: (Pause.) Not ending it. The temper scares me though.
You mentioned things are difficult with your kids. Is keeping away from them partly about that temper?
model.why: Follows the cue about his children, gently

model.text: (Quiet.) I don’t trust myself round them. So I stay away.
That tells me you’re trying to protect them, at a cost to yourself. That isn’t a bad dad. With treatment the temper settles, and that’s something we can work towards.

Here’s what I suggest. There’s an NHS service just for veterans, Op COURAGE. They offer trauma-focused therapy that works for combat-related PTSD. I can refer you today, or you can call them yourself.
Veterans only? Not some bloke who’s never been anywhere?

Veterans only. They understand forces life. For the sleep I won’t give you sleeping tablets, because they don’t fix the dreams and they’re easy to get hooked on. If you want medication alongside therapy, there’s an antidepressant that helps PTSD symptoms and isn’t addictive.
model.why: Avoids hypnotics; offers NG116 drug option

model.text: For the back, keep moving, and an anti-inflammatory for short spells can help, not strong painkillers long term. And the drink: would you be willing to cut back, with some support? It’s feeding the temper and the dreams.
model.why: NG59 back advice and alcohol negotiated

model.text: I can try. Referral’s fine. Do it.

If the dark thoughts come, or you feel you might lose control with someone, call 999, or NHS 111 with the mental health option. Combat Stress also has a 24-hour helpline for veterans. I’ll call you in two weeks myself.
So I know we’re on the same page, what are you taking away from this call?
Op COURAGE referral. Cut back the drink. No sleeping pills. Ring if it gets bad. You ring me in two weeks.
Spot on. And you won’t be passed around; I’m your point of contact. Anything else?
No. Cheers, doc.

social.t: Loss of structure, identity and comradeship after service. Veterans’ organisations (for example Combat Stress and Veterans’ Gateway) offer peer and practical support.
A warning at work and estrangement from his children. Treatment of the anger protects both; family contact can be rebuilt over time.

legal.t: PTSD can count as a disability if it has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities. His employer must then consider reasonable adjustments; a fit note can suggest them.
If his symptoms or drinking affect safe driving, he must notify the DVLA (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). Advise him not to drive after drinking or when exhausted.
If he describes a risk of harm to his children, follow local safeguarding procedures (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026, DfE).

professional.t: Veterans should face no disadvantage in accessing NHS care. Record veteran status so services such as Op COURAGE can be offered.
Being “passed around” drives disengagement. Name a clinician and book the follow-up before the call ends.

community.t: Op COURAGE (self-referral or GP referral); Combat Stress 24-hour helpline; NHS 111 mental health option; local alcohol service.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans or access to means
Risk of harm to others, including his children, from escalating anger
Back pain red flags: saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, leg weakness, fever, weight loss
psychosocial: Warning at work; relationship breakdown; estranged from his children
Military identity and distrust of services
ice: Idea: his problems are physical and fixable with tablets
Concern: needing help means he is “broken”; fear of his own anger around his kids
Expectation: painkillers and sleeping tablets, without being passed on again

playbook.diagnosis: “The dreams, the flashbacks, being on guard and the temper fit PTSD. It’s a common reaction to what you went through on tour, and it’s treatable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as your alarm system stuck on. It kept you alive on tour, but it hasn’t switched off since you came home. That’s why you can’t sleep and your fuse is short. Therapy helps reset it.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something practical and you didn’t want to be passed around. So: one referral to the right people, and I stay your contact.”
management.psychosocial: Alcohol reduction with support, a fit note or employer adjustments if needed, and a long-term aim of safe contact with his children.
sharedPlan: Op COURAGE referral for trauma-focused CBT (NICE NG116)
No hypnotics or opioids; sertraline or venlafaxine if he wants medication
Back: keep active, short NSAID courses if suitable (NICE NG59); cut back alcohol
safetyNet: 999 or NHS 111 mental health option if suicidal or at risk of harming someone; Combat Stress helpline
GP call in two weeks; face-to-face if back red flags develop

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by treating the back and the sleep at face value, or by rushing a guarded veteran into “mental health” talk before earning his trust.

items.fail: Prescribing codeine for the back and zopiclone for sleep.
items.why: “Did not identify the underlying problem” and “prescribing not in line with guidance” (NICE NG59; NICE NG116).
items.fix: Ask what wakes him; screen for nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance.

items.why: NICE NG116 recommends EMDR for non-combat-related trauma, not combat-related trauma.
items.fix: Offer trauma-focused CBT via Op COURAGE.

items.fail: No questions about suicide or harm to others.
items.why: “Risk not assessed.” Veterans with anger and heavy drinking need both asked directly.
items.fix: “Have you had thoughts of ending your life, or of seriously hurting someone?”

items.fail: “I think you have a mental health problem” in the first two minutes.
items.why: He has told you he distrusts “head stuff”. Pushing early loses him and the Relating marks.
items.fix: Start with the back and sleep, earn trust, then name PTSD as an injury.

items.fail: Not following up the comment about his children.
items.why: “Did not respond to cues.” It is the heart of his hidden agenda.
items.fix: “Is keeping away from them partly about the temper?” Then reframe it as protecting them.

items.fail: “The veterans service will be in touch” and nothing more.
items.why: He has been passed around before; a vague handover repeats it.
items.fix: A named contact, a set call-back date, crisis routes and teach-back.

timeMap.d: Short, practical, no feelings talk. Promise not to pass him around.
Back red flags. What wakes him? Nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance, alcohol.

timeMap.h: Name it and ask about risk
timeMap.d: PTSD as an injury. Suicide and harm to others. The children, gently.
Op COURAGE, trauma-focused CBT, no hypnotics or opioids, optional antidepressant, back advice, alcohol.
999, NHS 111 mental health option, Combat Stress, GP call in two weeks, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes codeine and zopiclone; never asks about nightmares or service; no risk questions; or pushes “mental health” early and loses him.
wordPics.pass: Recognises PTSD; asks about suicide and harm to others; refers to Op COURAGE or talking therapy; avoids hypnotics; addresses alcohol; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: engages him on his own terms; reframes PTSD as an injury; gently uncovers why he stays away from his children; knows trauma-focused CBT is the NG116 therapy for combat trauma; offers continuity so he isn’t passed around; checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like you need to see a psychiatrist.”
avoid.instead: “There’s an NHS service just for veterans. They get this, and their therapy works.”
avoid.why: “Psychiatrist” lands as “you’re broken”; a veteran service lands as respect.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you some sleeping tablets to break the cycle.”
avoid.instead: “Sleeping tablets won’t stop the dreams and they’re easy to get hooked on. Let’s treat what’s waking you.”
avoid.why: Hypnotics do not treat PTSD and add dependence risk, especially with alcohol.

avoid.instead: “It sounds like the drink is how you switch off. Would you be willing to cut back, with some help?”
avoid.why: An order invites resistance; a negotiated step is more likely to happen.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG59 (low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated 2026) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders, 2011) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · Op COURAGE (NHS England veterans’ mental health service)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoidance and anger since leaving the Army, presenting as back pain and insomnia, is probable PTSD. Assess risk, offer trauma-focused therapy through Op COURAGE, treat the drinking, and avoid dependence-forming drugs.

points.t: Re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance (crowds, news), hyperarousal (hypervigilance, startle, irritability, poor sleep) and emotional numbing after trauma. Veterans often present with pain, sleep, anger or alcohol and avoid “mental health” words.

NICE NG116: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to adults with PTSD. EMDR is recommended for PTSD after non-combat-related trauma; NG116 does not recommend it for combat-related trauma, where the evidence did not show benefit.

NICE NG116: consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline if the person prefers drug treatment. NG116 advises against drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD. Hypnotics and opioids do not treat PTSD and add dependence risk.
Op COURAGE is the NHS mental health service for veterans in England. Veterans can self-refer or be referred by their GP. Record veteran status on the notes.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and means, and about the risk of harm to others given the escalating anger, including any contact with his children. Heavy drinking raises impulsivity. NICE NG225 advises against risk scales to decide care.

Screen back pain red flags. NICE NG59: do not offer opioids for chronic low back pain; consider an oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with exercise. Quantify alcohol with AUDIT-C; NICE CG115 for assessment and specialist referral if dependent.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Accepted his practical framing and his wish not to be passed around; open question into the sleep.
Work warning, relationship breakdown, estrangement from his children, alcohol, military identity.
Picked up “bad dreams”, the pause, and the comment about his kids, and explored each.
Idea (physical problems needing tablets); concern (being “broken”, his anger around his children); expectation (painkillers and sleeping tablets).
Back red flags; AUDIT-C; a validated PTSD screen can support the referral; face-to-face back examination if red flags or new features.
PTSD; depression; alcohol use disorder; mechanical back pain versus serious spinal pathology.
Suicide and harm to others asked directly; back red flags excluded.
Names probable PTSD as an injury, not weakness, and links the sleep, anger and drinking to it.
Op COURAGE and trauma-focused CBT; no hypnotics or opioids; optional SSRI or venlafaxine; NG59 back advice.
Alcohol reduction with support; work pressures; family relationships.
999, NHS 111 mental health option, Combat Stress helpline, GP call in two weeks, named contact.

social.t: Loss of structure, identity and comradeship after service. Veterans’ organisations (for example Combat Stress and Veterans’ Gateway) offer peer and practical support.
A warning at work and estrangement from his children. Treatment of the anger protects both; family contact can be rebuilt over time.

legal.t: PTSD can count as a disability if it has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities. His employer must then consider reasonable adjustments; a fit note can suggest them.
If his symptoms or drinking affect safe driving, he must notify the DVLA (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). Advise him not to drive after drinking or when exhausted.
If he describes a risk of harm to his children, follow local safeguarding procedures (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026, DfE).

professional.t: Veterans should face no disadvantage in accessing NHS care. Record veteran status so services such as Op COURAGE can be offered.
Being “passed around” drives disengagement. Name a clinician and book the follow-up before the call ends.

community.t: Op COURAGE (self-referral or GP referral); Combat Stress 24-hour helpline; NHS 111 mental health option; local alcohol service.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans or access to means
Risk of harm to others, including his children, from escalating anger
Back pain red flags: saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, leg weakness, fever, weight loss
psychosocial: Warning at work; relationship breakdown; estranged from his children
Military identity and distrust of services
ice: Idea: his problems are physical and fixable with tablets
Concern: needing help means he is “broken”; fear of his own anger around his kids
Expectation: painkillers and sleeping tablets, without being passed on again

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The dreams, the flashbacks, being on guard and the temper fit PTSD. It’s a common reaction to what you went through on tour, and it’s treatable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as your alarm system stuck on. It kept you alive on tour, but it hasn’t switched off since you came home. That’s why you can’t sleep and your fuse is short. Therapy helps reset it.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted something practical and you didn’t want to be passed around. So: one referral to the right people, and I stay your contact.”
management.psychosocial: Alcohol reduction with support, a fit note or employer adjustments if needed, and a long-term aim of safe contact with his children.
sharedPlan: Op COURAGE referral for trauma-focused CBT (NICE NG116)
No hypnotics or opioids; sertraline or venlafaxine if he wants medication
Back: keep active, short NSAID courses if suitable (NICE NG59); cut back alcohol
safetyNet: 999 or NHS 111 mental health option if suicidal or at risk of harming someone; Combat Stress helpline
GP call in two weeks; face-to-face if back red flags develop

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by treating the back and the sleep at face value, or by rushing a guarded veteran into “mental health” talk before earning his trust.

items.fail: Prescribing codeine for the back and zopiclone for sleep.
items.why: “Did not identify the underlying problem” and “prescribing not in line with guidance” (NICE NG59; NICE NG116).
items.fix: Ask what wakes him; screen for nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance.

items.why: NICE NG116 recommends EMDR for non-combat-related trauma, not combat-related trauma.
items.fix: Offer trauma-focused CBT via Op COURAGE.

items.fail: No questions about suicide or harm to others.
items.why: “Risk not assessed.” Veterans with anger and heavy drinking need both asked directly.
items.fix: “Have you had thoughts of ending your life, or of seriously hurting someone?”

items.fail: “I think you have a mental health problem” in the first two minutes.
items.why: He has told you he distrusts “head stuff”. Pushing early loses him and the Relating marks.
items.fix: Start with the back and sleep, earn trust, then name PTSD as an injury.

items.fail: Not following up the comment about his children.
items.why: “Did not respond to cues.” It is the heart of his hidden agenda.
items.fix: “Is keeping away from them partly about the temper?” Then reframe it as protecting them.

items.fail: “The veterans service will be in touch” and nothing more.
items.why: He has been passed around before; a vague handover repeats it.
items.fix: A named contact, a set call-back date, crisis routes and teach-back.
